title: Identifiable elicitation complexity
formal: Determine the identifiable elicitation-complexity function \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) defined below, throughout its full domain of nonempty convex families of real-outcome distributions and finite-dimensional statistical properties. Its value is the smallest positive number of intermediate real reports needed to recover \(\Gamma\) through an elicitable, identifiable property, or \(\infty\) if no finite number suffices. The numerical benchmark requires a real-valued approximation with absolute error at most \(1/100\) at every finite value, and a proof identifying exactly the infinite-value cases.
why: A loss can recover a richer prediction than the statistic ultimately needed. The minimum dimension of that prediction measures an expressive limitation of loss-based estimation, independently of optimization time. A general classification would connect statistical functionals, forecast evaluation and the design of indirect prediction objectives.
status_note: Question 3 is open in the 2016 source. The checked 2021 journal framework proves important families of complexity bounds, and the 2024 survey still lists unresolved examples. Bounded later checks through 2026-09-16 verified no classification over the full stated domain; restricted Lipschitz and calibration variants are not treated as resolving it.

progress.text: Question 3 asks for a characterization of the elicitation complexity classes, with identifiable intermediate properties specified in Section 3.

The journal study develops complexity relative to several classes of intermediates and gives upper and lower bounds that match for important families. Its Definitions 2, 4, 6 and 7 specify elicitation, relative complexity and identification.
A survey by Frongillo and Waggoner describes further open complexity questions and distinguishes ordinary single-observation elicitation from multi-observation and conditional variants.

sentences: The question asks how many real-valued reports are needed to recover an arbitrary statistic by minimizing expected loss.
The intermediate prediction must have a unique expected-loss minimizer and an identification function whose expected value vanishes exactly at the correct report.
An unrestricted link may then turn that intermediate prediction into the desired statistic.
The target covers every finite-dimensional property of a nonempty convex family of real-outcome distributions, with infinity meaning that no finite report dimension works.
A full classification would determine the expressive limits of single-observation loss-based prediction beyond the statistic families whose complexities are already known.

definitions:
Let \(\mathcal M\) be the set of Borel probability measures on \(\mathbb R\). A distribution family \(\mathcal P\) is any nonempty subset of \(\mathcal M\) that contains \(\lambda p+(1-\lambda)q\) whenever \(p,q\in\mathcal P\) and \(0\le\lambda\le1\). The domain consists of every such \(\mathcal P\), every positive integer \(d\), and every function \(\Gamma:\mathcal P\to\mathbb R^d\). The dimension \(d\) is part of the specification of \(\Gamma\). No finite encoding, computability, continuity, moment assumption or uniform support bound is imposed on this domain.

For a positive integer \(k\), an admissible intermediate property consists of a nonempty report set \(R\subseteq\mathbb R^k\), a surjective function \(h:\mathcal P\to R\), a loss \(L:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\), an identification function \(V:R\times\mathbb R\to\mathbb R^k\), and a link \(\psi:R\to\mathbb R^d\). For each report \(r\in R\), the functions \(y\mapsto L(r,y)\) and every coordinate of \(y\mapsto V(r,y)\) must be Borel measurable and absolutely integrable with respect to every \(p\in\mathcal P\). Write \(\mathbb E_p u(Y)=\int_{\mathbb R}u(y)\,dp(y)\). Elicitation means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and every \(r\in R\) distinct from \(h(p)\), \(\mathbb E_p L(h(p),Y)<\mathbb E_p L(r,Y)\). Thus the expected loss has the unique global minimizer \(h(p)\), with no approximate minimization or tie-breaking convention. Identification means that, for every \(p\in\mathcal P\) and \(r\in R\), \(\mathbb E_p V(r,Y)=0\) if and only if \(h(p)=r\). Finally, \(\Gamma(p)=\psi(h(p))\) must hold for every \(p\in\mathcal P\).

Set \(E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\) to the least positive integer \(k\) for which these objects exist, and to \(\infty\) when there is no such finite \(k\). The unit is the number of scalar real coordinates of the intermediate report. Constant properties therefore have value \(1\), under the positive-dimension convention used here. Requiring \(R=h(\mathcal P)\) makes identification apply exactly to attainable reports; unused reports can be removed without losing elicitation. Neither convexity nor smoothness of \(L\), nor continuity of \(h\) or \(\psi\), is required. The single observation \(Y\) is the sole outcome argument of the loss and identification functions; a loss on several independent observations defines a different model. Statistical sample complexity and computational time for optimizing a loss are not the quantity being measured.

The symbol \(\infty\) here records failure of every finite report dimension. It does not assert the existence of a countably infinite-dimensional elicitable intermediate property. This convention extends the finite complexity classes to a total extended-valued function, including cases that the 2021 source leaves undefined when no allowed intermediate property exists.
answer_criterion: Give a complete mathematically correct Lean proof of a full determination of \(E\) on the stated domain: specify an unambiguous function \(a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)\in[0,\infty]\), prove \(a=\infty\) exactly when \(E=\infty\), and prove \(|a(\mathcal P,\Gamma)-E(\mathcal P,\Gamma)|\le1/100\) for every finite value, interpreting the integer \(E\) as a real number. A structural characterization of all finite complexity classes together with all infinite cases may specify the answer. The approximation need not be integer-valued, and no efficient algorithm or predetermined formula grammar is required. Merely repeating the defining minimum over admissible losses and intermediate properties, a one-sided bound, or a classification of only selected statistics does not meet the criterion.

context_blocks.text: The 2016 paper poses three distinct questions: which properties are elicitable, which losses elicit a given property, and how to characterize elicitation complexity classes. This card selects Question 3. It makes the real-outcome, convex-distribution-family branch explicit and retains the source’s restriction to identifiable intermediate properties; it does not additionally demand a classification of every possible loss.

Without a restriction on intermediate properties, encodings of an entire distribution into one real report can make the dimension measure degenerate. Identifiability is part of the target definition, rather than an optional regularity assumption.

The later journal treatment distinguishes identifiable intermediates from other classes defined through linear expectations or smooth convex losses. Its theorems establish tight complexity values for several families, including suitable Bayes-risk examples, rather than a classification of all statistical properties.

The 2024 survey still records unresolved elicitation complexities for several statistical quantities, including higher central moments and financial risk measures. Results using multiple independent observations or a restricted class of losses concern different complexity functions.
